Foundations of Government: Government
The institutions and processes through which a society is governed
Democracy
A system where political power ultimately rests with the people
Republic
A system where citizens elect representatives to govern on their behalf
Natural rights
Rights to life, liberty, and property that government does not grant
Social contract
The theory that people consent to be governed in exchange for protection
Popular sovereignty
The principle that government authority comes from the people
Limited government
The principle that government power is restricted by law
Rule of law
The principle that everyone, including leaders, is subject to the law
Direct democracy
Citizens vote on laws themselves rather than through representatives
Autocracy
Rule by a single person with unchecked power
The Constitution and Federalism: Constitution
The supreme law establishing the structure and limits of government
Preamble
The opening statement of the Constitution's purposes
Separation of powers
Dividing government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches
Checks and balances
Each branch's ability to limit the powers of the others
Federalism
Division of power between national and state governments
Enumerated powers
Powers specifically listed as belonging to the federal government
Reserved powers
Powers kept by the states under the Tenth Amendment
Concurrent powers
Powers shared by both federal and state governments, such as taxation
Supremacy clause
Federal law prevails when it conflicts with state law
Necessary and proper clause
Allows Congress laws needed to carry out its listed powers
Amendment process
Proposal by two thirds of Congress and ratification by three fourths of states
Ratification
Formal approval of the Constitution or an amendment
The Legislative Branch: The legislative branch, made up of the House and the Senate
Chamber with representation based on state population, two-year terms
Chamber with two members per state, six-year terms
The presiding officer and leader of the majority in the House
Extended Senate debate used to delay or block a vote
The Senate procedure to end a filibuster, requiring sixty votes
A smaller group that reviews and shapes bills before floor votes
Congress enacting a bill over a presidential veto with two thirds of both chambers
Drawing district lines to favour a party or group
The House's power to formally charge an official with misconduct
Congress's exclusive authority over federal spending
The Executive Branch: President
Head of state, head of government, and commander in chief
Electoral College
The body that formally elects the president, allocated by state
Cabinet
The heads of executive departments advising the president
Executive order
A presidential directive with the force of law over the executive branch
Veto
The president's power to reject a bill passed by Congress
Pocket veto
A bill dying when the president neither signs nor returns it as Congress adjourns
Commander in chief
The president's role as head of the armed forces
Executive privilege
The claimed right to withhold certain communications from other branches
Bureaucracy
The agencies and civil servants who carry out federal law
War Powers Resolution
Law limiting how long a president can commit troops without Congress
Twenty-Second Amendment
Limits a president to two elected terms
Pardon
The president's power to forgive a federal crime
The Judicial Branch: The highest federal court and final interpreter of the Constitution
The power to strike down laws that violate the Constitution
The authority to hear a case first, before any appeal
The authority to review decisions of lower courts
A prior decision that guides how similar cases are decided
The principle of standing by settled precedent
The Court's binding decision and its reasoning
A written disagreement by justices in the minority
An approach willing to overturn precedent or strike down laws
An approach deferring to elected branches wherever possible
The order by which the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case
Civil Liberties and the Bill of Rights: Civil liberties
Protections limiting what government may do to individuals
First Amendment
Protects religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
Establishment clause
Bars government from establishing an official religion
Free exercise clause
Protects the practice of religion from government interference
Fourth Amendment
Protects against unreasonable searches and seizures
Fifth Amendment
Protects against self-incrimination and double jeopardy, guarantees due process
Sixth Amendment
Guarantees a speedy public trial, counsel, and an impartial jury
Eighth Amendment
Bars excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishment
Due process
The requirement that government follow fair procedures
Miranda rights
Warnings police must give before custodial questioning
Exclusionary rule
Illegally obtained evidence cannot be used at trial
Clear and present danger
Standard historically used to limit speech posing immediate harm
Civil Rights: Protections against discrimination and guarantees of equal treatment
Fourteenth Amendment guarantee of equal treatment under law
1896 ruling upholding separate but equal segregation
1954 ruling that segregated schools are unconstitutional
Banned discrimination in employment and public accommodations
Outlawed literacy tests and other barriers to voting
Policies intended to remedy past discrimination in hiring or admissions
Segregation created and enforced by law
Segregation existing in practice without a law requiring it
Guaranteed women the right to vote
Lowered the voting age to eighteen
Political Parties and Elections: Political party
An organisation seeking to win elections and control government
Two-party system
A system dominated by two major parties
Third party
A minor party that rarely wins but can shift the debate
Primary election
An election choosing a party's nominee
Caucus
A local meeting where party members select a nominee
General election
The final election choosing who takes office
Platform
A party's formal statement of positions
Incumbent
The current officeholder, usually favoured for reelection
Swing state
A state where either party could plausibly win
Voter turnout
The share of eligible voters who actually vote
Campaign finance
The raising and spending of money in elections
Super PAC
A group that may raise unlimited money but not coordinate with a campaign
Interest Groups and Media: Interest group
An organisation seeking to influence policy on behalf of members
Lobbying
Directly pressing lawmakers to support a position
Political action committee
An organisation that raises and donates money to campaigns
Grassroots movement
Political pressure organised from ordinary citizens upward
Free rider problem
People benefiting from a group's work without contributing
Mass media
Channels reaching large audiences and shaping political awareness
Agenda setting
The media's power to influence which issues people consider important
Media bias
Slant in coverage favouring a viewpoint
Watchdog role
The press function of exposing wrongdoing in government
Public opinion poll
A survey measuring what the public thinks
Echo chamber
An information environment reinforcing what a person already believes
Iron triangle
The alliance of an agency, a congressional committee, and an interest group
Public Policy: Public policy
Government's chosen course of action on an issue
Domestic policy
Government action on matters inside the country
Foreign policy
Government's approach to relations with other nations
Fiscal policy
Using taxing and spending to influence the economy
Monetary policy
Federal Reserve control of money supply and interest rates
Entitlement program
A benefit guaranteed to everyone who qualifies, such as Social Security
Deficit
Spending more than revenue in a single year
National debt
The accumulated total of all past deficits
Regulation
A rule issued by an agency carrying the force of law
Policy agenda
The set of issues officials are actively considering
State and Local Government: State constitution
The founding legal document of an individual state
Governor
The chief executive of a state
State legislature
The lawmaking body of a state
Municipality
A city or town with its own local government
County
An administrative division of a state
Home rule
Authority granted to a locality to govern its own affairs
Initiative
A process letting citizens propose a law directly by petition
Referendum
A public vote on a measure passed by the legislature
Recall
A process letting voters remove an official before their term ends
School board
The elected body governing a local school district
Comparative Political Systems: Parliamentary system
The executive is drawn from and answerable to the legislature
Presidential system
The executive is elected separately from the legislature
Prime minister
Head of government in a parliamentary system
Unitary system
Power concentrated in a national government
Confederation
A loose union where member states keep most power
Authoritarianism
Concentrated power with limited political freedom
Totalitarianism
Government seeking control over nearly all aspects of life
Constitutional monarchy
A monarch serves as head of state within constitutional limits
Theocracy
Government where religious leaders rule and religious law governs
Coalition government
A government formed when several parties combine to hold a majority
